title: Control Flow
subtitle: The Ley Clock Decides
martuIntro:
The Ley Clock does not panic. It checks. If the hand is near the arc, it warns. Otherwise, it waits.
Today you teach Python to check the same way. And you learn to roll dice, because the world is not fair, yes?
You have seen this code already: the four dialogue options, the trap-door skill checks. It felt like a wall. Now we take it apart, one stone at a time.
goals: Ask yes-or-no questions with `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`, and get `True` or `False`
Choose `>=` on purpose, so exactly enough still passes
Compare text exactly, and with `.lower()` so capitals don't matter
Write `if`, `else` and `elif` with colons and indents, knowing the first true branch wins
Roll dice with `import random` and `random.randint(1, 20)`, both ends included
Read Python's error message, find the line, and mend it

questions.q: In `rope_count * rope_price`, which one is *how many*?

whyWrong.1: `rope_price` is how much one coil costs. `rope_count` is how many coils.

questions.explain: A cost is how many times the price of one: `rope_count` is how many, `rope_price` is the price of one.

exercises.title: True or False
exercises.martu:
A [[comparison]] is a yes/no question. Python answers [[True and False|True or False]], with no quotes.
`>` asks: is it more than? `<` asks: is it less than? The wide side of the sign faces the bigger number.
Guess first, then press Run.

anotherWay.label: A light switch
anotherWay.text:
A yes/no answer is a light switch: on or off, nothing in between.
```text
6 < 15   ->  [ON ]  True
6 > 15   ->  [OFF]  False
```

anotherWay.label: A yes/no question
anotherWay.text: "Are you taller than the door?" has only two answers: yes or no. A comparison is that kind of question. Python says `True` for yes and `False` for no.

`print(dex < needed)`:
1. Python looks inside the boxes: `6 < 15`.
2. It works out the question: is 6 less than 15? Yes.
3. It prints the answer: `True`.
A comparison is a question. Python answers `True` or `False`.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? No quotes
anotherWay.text: `True` has no quotes. It is not a word to show; it is Python's own yes. `"True"` with quotes is just four letters of text, like `"glug"`.

exercises.title: Asking with ==
exercises.martu:
`=` puts a value in a box: read it as *gets*. `==` asks a question: read it as [[is the same as]].
So `clock_is_red = (clock_color == "red")` reads: `clock_is_red` gets the answer to *is* `clock_color` *the same as red?*
Python works out the question in brackets first. Then the answer goes in the box.

anotherWay.label: Fill or ask
anotherWay.text:
```text
is_lucky = ...
[ is_lucky ] <- answer

hero == "Lucky"
[ hero ] ? "Lucky"
```
The first line fills a box: one `=` points into it. The second only asks: two `==` put a question mark between two things.

anotherWay.label: Name tag or question
anotherWay.text: Writing your name on a name tag is `=`: you put something there. Asking "Are you Lucky?" is `==`: you only want a yes or a no.

anotherWay.label: Right side first
anotherWay.text:
`is_lucky = (hero == "Lucky")`:
1. Python looks at the right side first: is `hero` the same as `"Lucky"`?
2. `hero` holds Bomb Shell, so the answer is `False`.
3. Then `is_lucky` gets that answer.
`=` puts; `==` asks.

exercises.title: Enough to pass
exercises.martu:
`>=` means [[at least]]. A roll of exactly the number needed still passes. `<=` means *at most*.
`>` is stricter: it leaves the number itself out. So `15 > 15` is False, but `15 >= 15` is True.
From here on, no brackets: `can_buy = coins >= price` works the same. Python asks the question first, then fills the box.

anotherWay.label: A number line
anotherWay.text:
The filled dot is the number needed. `>=` starts on the dot. `>` starts just after it.
```text
          13   14   15   16   17
roll >= 15            ●=========>
roll > 15             o====>
```

anotherWay.label: Try 14, 15, 16
anotherWay.text:
```text
roll | roll > 15 | roll >= 15
 14  |  False    |  False
 15  |  False    |  True
 16  |  True     |  True
```
Only the 15 row is different. That row is the boundary.
A 15 opens a latch that needs 15. Bomb Shell does not need 16. Exactly enough is enough.
Exactly enough counts? Use `>=`.

campaignLink.why: You have seen this line at the trap door. `roll >= required_roll` asked: is the roll at least the number needed? It handed back `True` or `False`. A roll of exactly 15 opened a latch that needed 15.

exercises.takeaway: `>=` means *at least*: exactly enough still passes. `>` leaves the number itself out.

predict.q: The latch needs 15. Which rolls pass? What will this print?
predict.explain: 14 is one short: `False`. 15 is exactly enough: `True`, because `>=` counts the number itself. 16 is more than enough: `True`. With `>`, the 15 would fail.

exercises.pairTalk: Pair talk: explain to your partner why a 15 should open a latch that needs 15. Which sign says that? Then each of you writes your own lines.

exercises.title: Any case, same answer
exercises.martu:
`"YES" == "yes"` is False: every letter, space and capital counts.
The dot means: ask this text to do something. `answer.lower()` gives a [[.lower()|lower-case copy]] of `answer`. The `()` at the end makes it run.
The copy is new. The text in `answer` does not change.

anotherWay.label: A copy in small letters
anotherWay.text:
```text
answer         -> "YeS"
answer.lower() -> "yes"
"yes" == "yes" -> True
```
`answer` stays the same. `answer.lower()` is a new copy in small letters.

anotherWay.label: A kind librarian
anotherWay.text: A librarian who ignores capitals finds your book whether you write HARRY or harry. `.lower()` makes Python that kind of librarian: it compares small letters with small letters.

`said_yes = answer.lower() == "yes"`:
1. `answer.lower()` makes a copy in small letters: `"yes"`.
2. Python asks: is `"yes"` the same as `"yes"`? `True`.
3. `said_yes` gets `True`.
Small letters on both sides: `answer.lower() == "yes"`.

exercises.martu:
Three bugs. Two are loud: Python stops and names a line. One is quiet: the code runs, but a box holds the wrong kind of thing.
Read the last line of Python's message first. Then look at the line it names. Mend it, run again, and see what Python finds next.

exercises.title: If
exercises.martu:
An [[if]] asks a question. When the answer is `True`, Python runs the [[indent|indented]] lines under it. When it is `False`, Python skips them.
The `if` line ends with a [[colon]]. The lines that belong to it start with four spaces.
Run it. Then change `hours_left` to 10 and run again. Why does nothing print?

anotherWay.label: A fork in the road
anotherWay.text:
```text
hours_left < 3 ?
   True  -> run the indented lines
   False -> skip them, go on
```
The `if` is a fork. The question decides which way Python walks.

anotherWay.label: If it rains
anotherWay.text: If it rains, take the umbrella and wear boots. No rain? You skip both. The indented lines are the things you do only when it rains.

anotherWay.label: Step table
anotherWay.text:
With `hours_left = 10`:
1. `hours_left = 10`: the box holds 10.
2. `if hours_left < 3:` asks: is 10 less than 3? `False`.
3. Python skips every indented line under the `if`.
4. Nothing prints.

anotherWay.label: The barrier door
anotherWay.text: My barrier door opens only if the hours are short. Long hours, the door stays shut, and the lines behind it never happen.

exercises.title: Colon and indent
exercises.martu:
Two marks make an `if` work. The [[colon]] at the end says: here comes the [[block]]. The indent says: this line belongs to it.
This spell has three slips. Python names the first two, one at a time. Read the last line of its message first. The third slip is quiet: the program runs, but one line is in the wrong place.

anotherWay.label: Colon, then indent
anotherWay.text:
1. The colon says: here comes the block.
2. The indent says: this line belongs to it.
3. The first line with no indent ends the block. It runs every time.

anotherWay.label: A shelf
anotherWay.text:
```text
if hours_left < 3:
    print("Shield up.")
print("The clock ticks on.")
```
The `if` line is the shelf, and `print("Shield up.")` sits on it. `print("The clock ticks on.")` is on the floor.
Indented lines sit on the `if`'s shelf. They fall only when the answer is True. The floor is always there.
Colon at the end of every `if` line. Four spaces for each line that belongs to it. No spaces: always runs.

exercises.title: Otherwise
exercises.martu:
[[else]] means otherwise. It has no question of its own. It runs when the `if` answer was `False`.
So exactly one of the two lines prints: the `if` block, or the `else` block. Never both.
Look at the Example: Oogrish's perception check. Then write Bomb Shell's latch check. Keep the starter's box names, `strength_roll` and `strength_needed`, and use your own words for the two lines.

anotherWay.label: Two doors
anotherWay.text:
```text
strength_roll >= strength_needed ?
   True  -> door 1: the if block
   False -> door 2: the else block
```
One question, two doors. Python walks through exactly one.

anotherWay.label: Coat or sunglasses
anotherWay.text: If it rains, take a coat. Otherwise, take sunglasses. You never take both, and you never take neither.

anotherWay.label: Try 11, 12, 13
anotherWay.text:
With `strength_needed = 12`:
1. A roll of 11: is 11 >= 12? `False`, so the `else` line prints.
2. A roll of 12: is 12 >= 12? `True`. Exactly enough passes.
3. A roll of 13: `True` too.
`if` question `:` then the success line. `else:` then the failure line.

checkpoints.text: Bomb Shell pries the latch. Print a success line when `strength_roll` reaches `strength_needed`, and a failure line otherwise.
hints: What question decides which line runs? Fill the `___` after `if` with it. Then replace each `___` in the quotes with your own words.

`else:` has no question. It runs when the `if` didn't:
```python
if coins >= price:
    print("Sold.")
else:
    print("Not enough coins.")
```
Exactly enough passes: a 12 opens a latch that needs 12. That is `>=`, not `>`.
Put `strength_roll >= strength_needed` in place of the `___` after `if`, so the line reads `if strength_roll >= strength_needed:`. Then put your own words in each `print`.

[[elif]] means else, if. Python checks the branches from the top and takes the *first* true one. Then it skips the rest.
My Ley Clock glows red when 2 hours or fewer are left, bright blue up to 12 hours, and calm blue after that. Someone wrote this chain in the wrong order. Which hours get the wrong color?

anotherWay.label: The chain, top to bottom

```text
<= 2 ?   yes -> red          (stop)
  no
<= 12 ?  yes -> bright blue  (stop)
  no
else         -> calm blue
```

anotherWay.label: Trace 2, 7 and 20
anotherWay.text:

2. 7 hours: `7 <= 2` is False. `7 <= 12` is True. Bright blue. Stop.
3. 20 hours: both False, so the `else`: calm blue.
First true branch wins. So first, the test that lets the fewest numbers through: `<= 2`, then `<= 12`, then `else`.

exercises.title: And, or, not
exercises.martu:
Three small words join questions.
[[and]]: both must be `True`. To cast, Oogrish needs enough mana and enough affinity.
[[or]]: one is enough. Lucky passes if his first roll or his second roll is high enough.
[[not]]: flips the answer. `not True` is `False`.

anotherWay.label: A truth table with the real stats
anotherWay.text:
Oogrish: mana 12, cost 9, affinity 9, needs 9.
1. `mana >= cost`: 12 >= 9, True.
2. `affinity >= required`: 9 >= 9, True.
3. True `and` True: True. He casts.
With only 5 mana: False `and` True is False. With `or`, it would be True, and he would cast with no mana. Bad.

anotherWay.label: Keys
anotherWay.text: `and` is a door with two locks: you need both keys. `or` is two doors: either key gets you in.

anotherWay.label: Two lamps
anotherWay.text:
```text
and: [on]  [on]  -> on
and: [on]  [off] -> off
or:  [on]  [off] -> on
or:  [off] [off] -> off
not: [on]        -> off
```
`and` needs both. `or` needs one. `not` flips.

exercises.martu:
The world is not fair, so we roll. [[import]] `random` lends you Python's dice.
`random.randint(1, 6)` ([[randint]]) gives a whole number from 1 to 6, *both ends included*. So 1 can come up, and 6 can come up. 0 and 7 never do.

items.body:
There is another way to write the four-answers chain. It is called [[match]].
`match choice:` says: look at what is in `choice`. Each `case "option 1":` says: if it is these exact letters, run the lines under me. `case _:` catches anything else, like `else`.
Python tries the cases from the top and runs the first one that fits. Then it stops, the same as `elif`.
The two examples below print the same line. Run both and compare them.
The campaign uses `elif`, so learn to read both. When you write your own, use whichever reads more clearly to you.

exercises.title: A fifth option
exercises.martu: Here is the four-answers chain as a `match`, with `case _:` at the end for anything else. A fifth option appeared on the board. Give it a case of its own.

anotherWay.label: match next to elif
anotherWay.text:
With `elif`:
```text
if choice == "option 1":
elif choice == "option 2":
else:
```
With `match`:
```text
match choice:
    case "option 1":
    case "option 2":
    case _:
```
Same choices, two ways to write them. Each `if` or `elif` line becomes a `case` line, and `else:` becomes `case _:`.

items.title: Ley Clock Quiz
items.summary: Eight questions on comparisons, if/elif/else, and and/or, and dice. Retake as often as you like.

questions.explain: `>=` means at least: 12 is at least 12, so True. `>` leaves the boundary out: 12 is not more than 12.
`2 <= 2` is True, so the first branch runs. Only one branch of a chain ever runs.

whyWrong.0: `randint` starts at the first number you give it: 1, not 0.
whyWrong.1: `randint` includes both ends, so 6 can come up.
whyWrong.3: 0 is below the first number, so it never comes up.

questions.explain: `random.randint(1, 6)` gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. Both ends are included, like a real d6.
Enough mana (12 >= 9), but affinity 8 is below 9. `and` needs both, so False.

questions.q: Put the lines in order (with their indents) so the program prints Mar'tu's reply to option 2.
lines: print("The decay? The clock is speeding up.")
print("It turned red once. Never again, I hope.")
questions.expectedOutput: The decay? The clock is speeding up.
questions.explain: One `if`, then `elif`s, in order. Each option is text, so it keeps its quotes.

questions.q: This should print `A perfect roll!` for a 20. Mend it.
questions.explain: `=` puts a value in a box. An `if` asks, so it needs `==`: is the same as.

questions.q: Which line asks whether `hero` is Lucky?

whyWrong.0: `=` puts Lucky in the box. It does not ask anything.
whyWrong.2: With no quotes, Python looks for a box named `Lucky`. The name is text, so it needs quotes.
whyWrong.3: With quotes, `"hero"` is the word hero, not the box. That asks whether two different words match.

questions.explain: `hero == "Lucky"` asks: is the text in the box `hero` the same as these exact letters?

choices:
A good roll.
A great roll.
questions.explain: `18 >= 10` is True, so the first branch wins and the rest are skipped, even though 18 is also great. The order rule: first, the test that lets the fewest numbers through. `>= 15` lets fewer numbers through than `>= 10`, so it goes first.

items.title: Road Encounter Table
items.summary: Roll a d20 and see what the road to the old Institute throws at you. You write the encounters.
items.intro:
The road to the old Institute is long. Oogrish insists on an encounter table: roll a d20, and the table says what the road throws at you. You write the encounters.
Three parts, in order: A. roll, B. the table, C. tell it.
The tiers: 1, then 2 to 6, 7 to 15, 16 to 19, and 20. The first two branches are started for you. Any words you like for each tier.
items.martu:
Oogrish is right, as usual. Roll first, then let the table decide, then say it out loud.
My check rolls the die for you, every number that matters, so it can see each tier. Your words stay yours.

anotherWay.label: The table
anotherWay.text:
```text
roll 1        -> tier 1
roll 2 to 6   -> tier 2
roll 7 to 15  -> tier 3
roll 16 to 19 -> tier 4
roll 20       -> tier 5
```
Each tier is one branch of the chain.

anotherWay.label: Trace a 6 and a 7
anotherWay.text:
1. A 6: `6 == 1`? No. `6 <= 6`? Yes: the ley-line tier. Stop.
2. A 7: `7 == 1`? No. `7 <= 6`? No. `7 <= 15`? Yes: the quiet road. Stop.

anotherWay.label: Oogrish's table
anotherWay.text: Oogrish keeps his tables on the back of a map, one tier per line, starting from the 1. The 20 is everything the other tiers did not catch, so it is the `else`.

items.title: Three Roads to the Institute
items.summary: Walk, ride Gearshift's jeep, or trust Lucky's Telegun? Work out each cost, then let the code pick the cheapest.
items.intro:
Mar'tu needs more brass instruments from the old Institute. Three ways to get there:
1. On foot: the party eats glug rations, more for a longer road.
2. Gearshift's jeep form: 2 coins of starlode a mile, plus 5 coins to start.
3. Lucky's Telegun: free on a good roll. On a roll under 15, Lucky lands in a hedge. Again.
Nobody agrees how far it is. So the code must pick the cheapest road for any `distance`.
items.martu:
Five parts, in order: A, B, C, D, E. Each part has its comment in the editor.
Work out what each road costs, then let the code choose. Mar'tu's check tries other distances and other rolls, so build every cost from the boxes, yes?
I counted everything in coins. Starlode, glug, hedges. Everything.

anotherWay.label: The three roads, side by side
anotherWay.text:
Costs in coins, with a Telegun roll under 15 (a hedge):
```text
miles  walk  jeep  Telegun
  5      8    15     18
 30     70    65     80
 80    150   165    160
```
On a roll of 15 or more, the Telegun column is 0, and it wins every time.

anotherWay.label: One part at a time
anotherWay.text:
1. A: three tiers, so `if`, `elif`, `else`. First, the test that lets the fewest numbers through.
2. B: one line, built from `distance`.
3. C: roll, then `if`/`else` on the roll.
4. D: ask *is walking the smallest?*, then *is the jeep smaller than the Telegun?*, then `else`.
5. E: glue `road` and `str(cost)` into one line.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: `cast_spell` in the barrier part picked one of three paths: not skilled enough, not enough mana, or cast. Python checked from the top and took the first true branch. Your road chooser works the same way.

items.title: When Spells Fizzle: Reading Errors
items.summary: Read Python's message like Mar'tu does: the last line, the line it names, and the values when there is no message.

exercises.title: Anatomy of a fizzle
exercises.martu:
When a spell fizzles, Python leaves you a note. The full note is a [[traceback]]. It looks scary. It is not. Three parts matter:
1. The last line: the error's name, then what went wrong.
2. The line number: where Python stopped.
3. The name or mark it is talking about.
Run Bomb Shell's spell. It fizzles on purpose. While the note is still on screen, write down what it says, in three boxes. Then switch line 4 off with `#` and Run again, so the rest can run. Good practice for boxes, too.

anotherWay.label: The note, with labels
anotherWay.text:
1. The last line, read it first: `NameError: name 'mana_cost' is not defined`. The first word, `NameError`, is the error's name.
2. Above it: `File "main.py", line 4`. That is the line where Python stopped.
3. Inside the little `'` marks: `mana_cost`, the name Python could not find.

anotherWay.label: Where to look, in order
anotherWay.text:
1. Read the last line first: the error's name, then what went wrong.
2. Then look at the line it names.
3. On that line, find the name or mark the message talks about.

anotherWay.label: A note on the door
anotherWay.text: It is like a note from a courier: *Could not deliver on line 4: nobody called mana_cost lives here.* The courier is not angry. The note says where, and what was missing.
Last line: the error's name and the missing name. Full message: the line number.

No message this time. The code runs. It just gives the wrong answer.

exercises.title: Syntax fizzles
exercises.martu:
Three slips that stop Python before anything runs: a quote, a colon, a bracket. Each one is a [[SyntaxError]]: Python could not read a line.
Guess first: three slips, so how many messages will you see? Press Run and count.
Then mend them one at a time, and read the new message after each Run.

anotherWay.label: Why only one message?
anotherWay.text: Python reads the whole program before it runs any of it. It stops at the first line it can't read, so it never gets to the other slips. Mend that one, run again, and it shows you the next. That is why errors come one at a time.

anotherWay.label: Python reads, then runs
anotherWay.text:
```text
Python reads every line.
Stuck on line 2?
  -> stop: one message.
All fine?
  -> run the program.
```
With a syntax slip, nothing runs at all. Not even line 1.
1. Run. 2. Read the last line. 3. Mend that one slip. 4. Run again: a new message is progress.
Quotes in pairs. Colon after `if`. Brackets in pairs.

Four [[NameError|NameErrors]]. Each one means: Python met a name that no line has made yet.
The causes differ: a typo, a box used too early, words without quotes, a capital letter. Read the last line each time. Sometimes Python even asks: *Did you mean ...?*

Fireball  words, no quotes
health    made as Health

3. No line makes it? Make it first, or fix the spelling, or add quotes if you meant words.

items.title: Mar'tu's Seal
items.summary: An `assert` line says what must be true. Seal your checks at the boundary, and quiet bugs get loud.
items.body:
At the Institute we sealed our work: a line that says what *must* be true. If it isn't, Python stops and tells you.
A seal is an [[assert]] line: the word `assert`, then a yes-or-no question. `assert passed == True` says: `passed` must be `True` here.
If the answer is `True`, nothing happens, and the program goes on. If it is `False`, Python stops with `AssertionError` and names the line:
```text
File "main.py", line 4
    assert passed == True
AssertionError
```
Why bother? Seals catch quiet [[bug|bugs]]. A `>` where `>=` belongs gives no error at all. A seal at the boundary turns that quiet bug into a loud one.
The campaign never asks for seals. They are for the careful, yes?

exercises.title: Seal the check
exercises.martu:
Three rolls against a `needed` of 15: one below, one exactly, one above. Under each one, write a seal that says what `passed` must be.
Then Mar'tu's check breaks your `passed` lines on purpose. Good seals catch it.

anotherWay.label: Three seals on a number line
anotherWay.text:
```text
   14        15        16
   fail  |  pass      pass
   ^          ^          ^
 False     True       True
```
The seal at exactly 15 is the one that catches `>`.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work?
anotherWay.text: `>` instead of `>=` gives no error: a quiet bug. A seal at the boundary says what must be true. When it is not, Python stops. The quiet bug becomes a loud one.
Below: `False`. Exactly: `True`. Above: `True`.

`cast_spell`, rebuilt. First `can_cast`: Oogrish needs enough mana *and* enough affinity. Then put the three lines in one chain, in the order the comments give. Exactly enough still casts. Mar'tu's check tries other spells, so ask with the boxes.
Stuck? Skip it, or try the lesson If the Clock Turns Red. Tasks you pass here stay ticked.

anotherWay.text:
```text
affinity lower? -> not skilled
  no
mana lower?     -> not enough mana
  no
else            -> the barrier holds
```
1. `can_cast`: two questions with `>=`, joined by `and`. 2. The chain: `if` affinity is lower, `elif` mana is lower, `else` cast. 3. Exactly enough? `9 < 9` is `False`, so it casts.

items.title: Quick Check 2 · Form A questions
items.summary: Four questions that go with Quick Check 2. To pass the Quick Check, get 3 of the 4 right.

questions.explain: `>=` means *at least*. 11 is not at least 12, but 12 is, and so is 13. Exactly enough passes.
18 is at least 15, so the first branch runs, and Python skips the rest. 18 is also at least 10, but only the first true branch runs. With 12 it would print `A hit.`, and with 4, `A miss.`

whyWrong.0: `randint` starts at the first number you give it: 1, not 0.
whyWrong.1: `randint` includes both ends, so 8 can come up too.
whyWrong.3: Both ends are included: 1 and 8. A d8 has no 0.

questions.explain: `random.randint(1, 8)` is a d8: any whole number from 1 to 8, both ends included.
`mana >= cost` is True, but `affinity >= required` is False: 9 is not at least 10. `and` needs both, so the brackets give False. `not` flips it: True. Oogrish can't cast this one yet.

items.title: Quick Check 2 · Form B questions
items.summary: Four questions that go with Quick Check 2. To pass the Quick Check, get 3 of the 4 right.

questions.explain: `<=` means *at most*. 1 and 2 are at most 2; 3 is not. Exactly 2 counts.
2 is at most 2, so the first branch runs, and Python skips the rest. 2 is also at most 12, but only the first true branch runs. With 12 it would print `bright blue`, and with 40, `calm blue`.

whyWrong.0: `randint` starts at the first number you give it: 1, not 0.
whyWrong.1: `randint` includes both ends, so 12 can come up too.
whyWrong.3: Both ends are included: 1 and 12. A d12 has no 0.

questions.explain: `random.randint(1, 12)` is a d12: any whole number from 1 to 12, both ends included.
`mana >= cost` is False: 26 is not at least 30. `affinity >= required` is True. `and` needs both, so the brackets give False. `not` flips it: True. Lucky is 4 mana short.

entries.note: No quotes: `True` and `False` are Python's yes and no. (Lesson: True or False, Yes?)
Read `=` as *gets* and `==` as *is the same as*. Every letter, space and capital counts.
`!=` is not the same as. `<` less than, `>` more than, `<=` at most, `>=` at least.
`>` leaves out the boundary. `>=` includes it, so exactly enough still passes.
`answer.lower()` gives a lower-case copy, so capitals stop mattering. Alone on a line, the copy is forgotten: keep it with `answer = answer.lower()`.
The colon says *here comes the block*. Four spaces say *this belongs to the if*. (Lesson: If the Clock Turns Red)
`else:` has no question. It runs when the `if` did not.
Python checks from the top and runs only the first true branch. So: first, the test that lets the fewest numbers through. `else` is always last.
`and` needs both. `or` needs one. `not` flips the answer.
`import random` once, at the top. `random.randint(1, 20)` gives 1 to 20, both ends included.
